newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan, Lebanon discuss deporting guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: Japan, Lebanon discuss deporting guerrillas.

text.p: Japan and Lebanon are discussing the deportation to Tokyo, possibly in a special plane, of five top members of the Red Army guerrilla group, authoritative sources said on Wednesday.
The sources also said Japanese embassies around the world had been urged to step up security in case of attacks in retaliation for the arrest of the five in Lebanon.
They said as well as the five guerrillas, Lebanese authorities were holding three other Japanese who were Red Army sympathisers and acted as go-betweens for them.
Several Lebanese were also in custody.
Official Lebanese sources have said the group was arrested in the Syrian-controlled Bekaa Valley in eastern Lebanon two days ago.
According to Lebanese officials the detainees included 49-year-old Kozo Okamoto, who was involved in the May 1972 shootout at Tel Aviv's Lod airport in which 24 people died and 100 were wounded.
Okamoto was captured by Israeli forces and sentenced to life imprisonment but was released in a Palestinian-Israeli prisoner swap in May, 1985.
Japanese media reports have named four of the detained guerrillas as Kazuo Tohira, 44, Hisashi Matsuda, 48, Mariko Yamamoto, 56, and Masao Adachi, 57.

The Red Army, founded in 1971, is allied to hardline anti-Israeli Palestinian factions. The Bekaa Valley was a haven during Lebanon's 1975-90 civil war for guerrilla groups including Lebanese Moslems and Marxists, Palestinians, Kurds and the Japanese Red Army.
The Red Army, which was also virulently anti-American and wanted the destruction of capitalism, staged spectacular hijackings, hostage-takings and other attacks during the 1970s and 1980s.
They were notorious for retaliatory action, three times launching attacks to force Japan into freeing jailed comrades.
In 1974, they seized the French Embassy in The Hague and won the release of one of their members, who went with them to Syria.

In 1975, the group seized the United States consul, the Swedish charge d'affaires and 51 other hostages in a building housing the U.S., Swedish, Japanese and Canadian embassies in Kuala Lumpur. They later won the release of five imprisoned comrades.

In 1977 five Red Army members hijacked a Japan Airlines airliner over India and forced it to land in Dhaka. The hijackers flew to Algeria after the Japanese government released six prisoners who joined them there.
"Police authorities in Japan will dispatch scores of officials to Lebanon to prepare for the deportation," the Asahi Evening News reported on Wednesday.
Precautions could include a special plane equipped with top security features to take the guerrillas from Beirut to Tokyo.
An advance Japanese security team, including officials who would handle the legal paperwork involved in an extradition, has already reached Beirut.
Japanese embassy officials and members of the security mission have met Lebanon's prosecutor-general Adnan Addoum to get the extradition proceedings going.
